messages.subject: Re: P1-P4 in iteminfo (type = 'info')
messages.body_plain:
I am not sure what it exactly is you want to know. The graph shows that for instance someone with an average latent trait level (theta = 0) has about .7 probability of endorsing the second respons category on item 1 (green curve). Where the lines crosses, the probability of another response increases. For instance it looks like that for someone with a latent trait level of 2 or above the probability of choosing the 4th response category is more likely as the curve of the 3th response category crosses below the curve of the 4th category at that point. I think MIRT counts the way your questions are keyed, i.e. from 0-4; higher score reflecting higher trait levels (if your questions are keyed this way)

Hope this helps

messages.subject: Re: P1-P4 in iteminfo (type = 'info')
messages.body_plain:
P1-P4 don't represent thresholds, these are the expected probability tracelines implied by your select IRT model for the item, and are associated with the respective categories in your item (P1 with the lowest category, while P4 would be the highest). Hence, they aren't information curves either. And the output you're printing is not demonstrating thresholds, but rather standardized factor loadings (if you want the actually parameters, use coef()).

Phil

messages.subject: Re: No plotdif returned
messages.body_plain:
This is a multidimensional model at its core, so generally plots supported for unidimensional model comparisons won't be available. The simple structure suggests that you could make plots though by focusing only on the unidimensional subsets though, but this will require some effort on your end to manipulate the returned model objects (which appears to be what you've done in the source code, so that's a start).

Phil

As I found the function iteminfo() in the mirt-documentary I just realized how to do what I wanted. Just in case anyone having the same issue, here is my solution:

The iteminfo() function gives you the item information-value for any specific theta. So I wrote a function that extracts a lot of theta values in a sequence for every item in a unidimensional mirt-model and copies it to an excel-sheet. You will need the xlsx-package for this.

CODE:
-----
install.packages("xlsx")
library(xlsx)

infoplot.to.xlsx <- function (model, path) { #the function needs a mirt-model as input as well as a path (string) in order to tell it where to save the xlsx
  thetas <- seq(-6, 6, 0.01) #creates a sequence of theta-values with 0.01 steps. I found that quite detailed, but you could alter that if you want.
  sheet <- cbind(thetas)

  for (i in 1:model@Data[["nitems"]]) {
    item <- extract.item(model, i)
    info <- iteminfo(item, Theta = thetas)
    sheet <- cbind(sheet, info)
  }

  sheet <- as.data.frame(sheet)
  names(sheet) <- c("Theta", paste("Item", 1:model@Data[["nitems"]], sep = "")) #renames the columns, so in your excel sheet you will now which column is which item...
  write.xlsx(sheet, file = path, sheetName = substitute(model))

}
-----

As I'm not much of a developer/programmer, I'm not quite sure if that's the best way to do it, but it worked for me. You get an xlsx-file, in which you can build and edit a custom linear-diagram from the extracted data. The results looked quite similar to the R-plot, so I think it's a valid way to do. Yet maybe Phil can confirm that or tell a better way to do :)

Stay healthy
Nick
